text:
I need to write an email asking for a higher fee. I'm a freelance illustrator and I've done 6 picture books for a children's publisher over the last 4 years. They just offered me their next book at the same fee as always.

Facts:
- They pay me $9,000 per book: 32 pages, about 14 full spreads. I've been at $9,000 since my first book with them.
- Each book takes me about 4 months.
- Two of my books with them have sold over 20,000 copies. One of those was on a state reading list.
- Another publisher paid me $12,500 last year for a book of the same length.
- My agent says $11,000 to $13,000 is normal for an illustrator with my record.
- I'd like $11,500 for this book.

I want to tell them every other publisher pays at least $12,000 for this kind of book. Keep it under 250 words.

Before I draft this, there's a problem with the line you most want to include. Your facts don't support "every other publisher pays at least $12,000." You have one other publisher at $12,500, and your agent's range starts at $11,000. If the editor knows anyone who has been paid less, and editors usually do, that one line makes the rest of the email look less credible. It also sits oddly next to a request for $11,500. I'd use what you can back up instead: another publisher paid you $12,500 last year for a book of the same length, and $11,000–13,000 is the normal range for your track record. That still makes your point, and $11,500 then looks modest. Tell me if you still want the original line.

A few questions so I can get the email right:

1. **Who's it going to?** What's the editor's first name, and how do you two usually write to each other (casual or more formal)? Also, are they the one who decides the fee, or will they have to take it to someone else?
2. **Which books did well?** I'd like to name the two that sold over 20,000 copies and the state reading list. Concrete titles are more convincing than "two of my books."
3. **Can I name the other publisher**, or should it just be "another publisher"?
4. **How firm is $11,500?** If they push back, would you still take the book at $9,000, or would you let it go? I won't say this in the email, but it changes how firm the wording should be.
5. **Is your agent involved?** If the agent normally handles fees, the email might need to say so, or come from them.

If you don't know some of these, just say so and I'll write it without them.

On the line: I still want it. If it goes past what I know, say it as strongly as you can without saying anything false.

1. It's going to Nadia Brooks, the managing editor. I'm not sure how formal we usually are, and I don't know if she decides the fee herself.
2. I don't have the titles to hand. The one on the state reading list went into its fourth printing this spring.
3. Just say "another publisher."
4. $11,000 is my lowest. I can't take it at $9,000, so I'd let it go. I don't have another offer for that slot, though, so I'd have a gap.
5. I don't know.

I left out the "every other publisher" line. You only know about one other publisher, so that would be stating something you can't back up. Here's the strongest true version: "The rate for this work is well above $9,000." The $12,500 fee and your agent's range come right after it to support it, and those are your strongest facts anyway.

<final_document>
Subject: Fee for the next book

Dear Nadia,

Thank you for offering me the next book. I've loved working with you over the past four years, and I'd very much like to do this one.

Before I accept, I need to raise the fee. I've been paid $9,000 per book since my first title with you, and six books later it's still the same. In that time, two of our books have sold more than 20,000 copies. One was chosen for a state reading list and went into its fourth printing this spring.

The rate for this work is well above $9,000. Last year another publisher paid me $12,500 for a book of the same length. My agent tells me $11,000 to $13,000 is the normal range for an illustrator with my record.

For this book I'm asking for $11,500. That's in the lower half of that range, and I think it fairly reflects what our books have done for your list. Each one takes me about four months, and I can't take on another at $9,000.

If this needs to go to anyone else for approval, I'm happy to send whatever would help. I hope we can make it work. I'd love to keep making books with you.

Best wishes,
[Your name]
</final_document>

About 215 words.

- **What's left out on purpose:** The email doesn't mention your $11,000 minimum or that you'd have a gap in your schedule. If Nadia offers less than $11,500, you can decide then whether to come down.
- **Tone:** It's warm but not casual, since you weren't sure how formal you two usually are.
- **Book titles:** If you find the titles before sending, put them in. "*[Title]* was chosen for the [State] reading list" is more convincing than "one was."
- **Your agent:** Check whether your agent normally handles fees before you send this. If they do, they may want to send it or be copied on it.
